title: Northpeak Search x Redwood — Dedicated Burst Capacity technical deep dive
summary: Technical deep dive on Redwood Dedicated “burst capacity” concept for Northpeak’s weekly indexing and launch spikes. Redwood walked through regional burst pools (per hardware class), admission control (max burst ratio, per-tenant caps, cooldowns), fairness (token bucket / weighted tiers), deterministic decisions under telemetry lag, routing behavior on deny (queue vs immediate), and observability (dashboards, denial reason codes, SLO gates, audit logs). Customer shared peak pattern: baseline H100 dedicated capacity with predictable 2–3x bursts for 1–2 hours, mostly us-east, with strict neighbor protection and clear customer-visible reporting. Closed with next steps: Redwood to share draft limits/reason codes, sample dashboards, and rough pricing/billing model; schedule follow-up with SRE + finance; Northpeak to provide workload profile (QPS, token distributions, concurrency) to size burst needs.
topics: Northpeak traffic profile: baseline vs peak multipliers (indexing jobs + product launches)
Burst pool model (per region + hardware class) and how it differs from permanent dedicated scaling
Admission control semantics: what counts as burst, when requests are denied, and cooldown windows
Fairness & noisy-neighbor protection: token bucket / tiering and anti-starvation behavior
Routing and client behavior on denial (429 vs queue/backpressure) + fallback expectations
Observability: burst usage, denials, saturation, and neighbor impact indicators (p95/p99 deltas)
Billing & metering: burst GPU-seconds / token accounting, idempotency on retries
Security/compliance: audit logging, RBAC, evidence for regulated customers
questions: Can we get a deterministic “yes/no” for burst at request time, or can it flip mid-stream?
Do you queue burst requests or do we get immediate 429s? If queued, what’s the max queue time?
Can we cap burst by project / workspace (not just tenant) so indexing can’t starve chat?
How do you prove we’re not hurting other tenants (and they’re not hurting us) during burst windows?
Is burst always within the same region and same GPU type (H100), or can it spill to L40S?
What shows up in audit logs if Support changes a cap or overrides a policy?
action_items: Redwood (Markus Klein): Send Northpeak a one-pager on burst admission semantics + denial reason codes (draft) by 2025-02-07
Redwood (Mina Haddad): Share sample Grafana screenshots/panels for burst saturation + denial reasons + neighbor impact (sanitized) by 2025-02-10
Redwood (Stephanie Nguyen): Coordinate a pricing/billing follow-up with Finance (Rishi/Laura) and propose a burst tier for 2–3x for 2 hours weekly by 2025-02-12
Customer (Sara Liu): Provide workload profile (baseline QPS, peak QPS, token distribution, concurrency, model choices) for indexing + online traffic by 2025-02-11
Customer (Jon Peters): Confirm preferred region/hardware constraints (us-east H100 only vs multi-region) and any SLO/SLA requirements by 2025-02-11
next_steps: Schedule 45-min follow-up: pricing + contract expectations for burst (include Northpeak procurement).
Schedule 30-min SRE/infra follow-up focused on SLO protection and rollback/circuit breaker behavior.
Northpeak sends workload profile so Redwood can suggest initial baseline + burst caps and a rollout/beta plan.
transcript:
Fireflies.ai Transcript

Meeting: Northpeak Search x Redwood — Dedicated Burst Capacity technical deep dive
Date: 2025-02-06
Start time: 9:00 AM PT
Duration: 54 minutes
Recorded by: Fireflies.ai

Attendees
- Stephanie Nguyen (Redwood) — AE
- Markus Klein (Redwood) — Solutions Engineering
- Mina Haddad (Redwood) — Smart Routing
- Amit Desai (Northpeak) — VP Engineering
- Sara Liu (Northpeak) — ML Platform Lead
- Jon Peters (Northpeak) — SRE/Infra
- Nina Patel (Northpeak) — Procurement (joined late)

Auto-summary (generated)
Northpeak described a need for temporary throughput increases without permanently resizing dedicated capacity. Redwood explained the shared, Redwood-managed burst pools per region/GPU class, the admission controller (policy + telemetry), fairness enforcement, and how routing responds to burst denial. The group aligned on requirements: deterministic behavior, explicit denial reasons, observability/reporting, and strict neighbor protection. Next steps were agreed for workload data exchange and pricing follow-up.

Topics
1) What “burst” means on Dedicated
2) Pool topology and guardrails
3) Determinism + telemetry lag handling
4) Metrics, dashboards, and alerting
5) Metering/billing and audit logs


Transcript

[00:00] Stephanie Nguyen: Cool. Alright, thanks everyone for joining. This is Stephanie from Redwood. Markus is on with me and Mina from routing. The goal today is to go deeper on the Dedicated burst capacity thing we teased last call.

[00:12] Amit Desai: Yep, thanks. We’ve got Sara and Jon. We’re basically trying to avoid buying a bunch of idle GPUs for one weekly spike.

[00:19] Markus Klein: Makes sense. And just to set expectations, this is still… like, we’re in design/early build. So I can be concrete about intended semantics, but we’ll call out what’s still moving.

[00:30] Sara Liu: That’s fine. We’re early too. We just need to know if it’s real and how it behaves when it’s not available.

[00:37] Mina Haddad: Yeah, “how it fails” is the most important part.

[00:40] Stephanie Nguyen: Exactly.

[00:43] Markus Klein: Before we jump in, quick context check. You’re looking at Dedicated, probably H100 in us-east, right?

[00:50] Sara Liu: Preferred. We run online query re-ranking and chat-ish stuff, but the spike is indexing. Indexing is mostly batch. It’s predictable.

[01:00] Jon Peters: And we don’t want it to tank p99 for the online tier. That’s like the whole thing.

[01:06] Markus Klein: Great. So bursting is basically: you have a reserved baseline—your dedicated pool. During a window you can temporarily exceed that baseline by borrowing from a separate Redwood-managed pool of GPUs, same region and same hardware class.

[01:21] Amit Desai: Borrowing like… other people’s unused dedicated?

[01:24] Markus Klein: No. Not from other dedicated reservations. It’s from a shared “burst pool” that Redwood provisions and owns. The point is we don’t violate isolation of dedicated baselines.

[01:34] Sara Liu: So it’s like overflow capacity that’s carved out.

[01:36] Markus Klein: Exactly. Think of it as a buffer that we can lend out under strict guardrails.

[01:42] Mina Haddad: And those guardrails are enforced by an admission controller in front of routing. Routing asks, “is tenant X allowed to burst right now for request Y?” and gets a deterministic response.

[01:54] Jon Peters: Deterministic meaning… if we retry the same request it’s the same answer?

[01:59] Mina Haddad: Within a short window, yes. We’re designing it so that if you hit us with retries you don’t get charged twice and you don’t see flappy admit/deny purely from jitter.

[02:11] Markus Klein: There’s two axes: per-tenant policy (your max burst ratio, your caps, cooldown) and global fleet safety (pool saturation and neighbor SLOs). Both can deny.

[02:23] Sara Liu: Define “burst ratio.”

[02:25] Markus Klein: Say your baseline is 16 H100 GPUs. A 2x burst ratio would allow you to go up to 32 GPUs worth of concurrent capacity, subject to pool availability and fairness.

[02:37] Amit Desai: And is that “for an hour” or “at any point”?

[02:41] Markus Klein: Good question. We’re modeling it as instantaneous cap plus optional time-based budgets. For initial release it’s primarily instantaneous: max burst cap + cooldown windows. We can also add time-slicing later.

[02:55] Jon Peters: Cooldown like… after we burst, we can’t burst again?

[02:58] Markus Klein: Not exactly. It’s more like, if you hit certain thresholds—like repeated admission denials or you’ve been above baseline for sustained time—we can throttle burst and force you to settle to baseline for a period.

[03:12] Sara Liu: So it’s kind of a circuit breaker but per tenant.

[03:15] Mina Haddad: Yeah, plus a global circuit breaker. If the burst pool is at risk of impacting non-burst tenants, we clamp burst across the board.

[03:25] Amit Desai: How do you measure “impacting” if we’re dedicated? Like aren’t we isolated?

[03:30] Mina Haddad: Your baseline is isolated. The burst pool is shared. If too many tenants borrow at once, queue times and tail latency can spike within the burst pool. Also, depending on routing topology, we can see knock-on effects at the gateway layer.

[03:45] Markus Klein: The rule we’re committing to is: bursting must not regress non-burst SLOs. So we have “neighbor impact” indicators—p95/p99 latency deltas for non-burst traffic—and SLO gates.

[03:58] Jon Peters: That’s what I wanted to hear, but… how strict is that? Like does one blip shut off everyone’s burst?

[04:05] Markus Klein: We’re aiming for measured gates. Example: if non-burst p95 goes +X% sustained for Y minutes AND correlated with burst saturation, we reduce burst caps or disable burst temporarily.

[04:17] Sara Liu: Can you share numbers?

[04:19] Markus Klein: Not final yet. We can share a starting point in writing—like a threshold proposal.

[04:24] Stephanie Nguyen: And to be clear we’d tune it in beta.

[04:28] Amit Desai: What’s the failure mode for us? Do we get 429s? Do you queue?

[04:34] Mina Haddad: That’s a key design point. We support two behaviors depending on endpoint: (1) immediate deny with a structured reason code, usually 429/overload; (2) bounded queue/backpressure where we accept but delay admission for a short time.

[04:51] Jon Peters: For streaming chat we can’t really queue.

[04:54] Mina Haddad: Right, for interactive chat the safest is immediate deny + client retry with jitter, or fallback to baseline-only behavior.

[05:04] Sara Liu: For indexing, queueing is fine if it’s bounded.

[05:07] Mina Haddad: Exactly. We can treat batch traffic differently. But we want semantics to be deterministic and explainable.

[05:15] Markus Klein: That’s why we’re standardizing denial reason codes. Examples: BURST_POOL_SATURATED, TENANT_BURST_CAP_REACHED, COOLDOWN_ACTIVE, FLEET_SAFETY_CLAMP, TELEMETRY_STALE.

[05:30] Amit Desai: Telemetry stale meaning you don’t know how many GPUs you have in use?

[05:34] Markus Klein: Or the utilization signal is delayed. We saw in early testing that delayed utilization can cause unfair denials. So we’re adding smoothing and “safe defaults” so we don’t oscillate.

[05:47] Jon Peters: “Safe default” usually means deny.

[05:50] Markus Klein: Sometimes, yes. But we can also do conservative admit. The tricky part is: we don’t want to over-admit and break the pool.

[05:59] Sara Liu: So what’s deterministic then if telemetry is stale?

[06:02] Mina Haddad: Determinism is: for a given tenant and a given request class, within a short evaluation interval, the policy engine returns the same decision, unless a hard safety event happens.

[06:13] Jon Peters: Like a global clamp.

[06:15] Mina Haddad: Exactly.

[06:18] Stephanie Nguyen: Maybe it’d help if we talk through your specific burst use case.

[06:22] Sara Liu: Sure. Weekly indexing job, every Tuesday 1 AM to 3 AM Eastern. Baseline we think is 8 H100s dedicated. During indexing we want 2–3x for about two hours. Then we drop back.

[06:39] Amit Desai: And occasionally we do launches where we have a day of heavier online.

[06:43] Markus Klein: Got it. For that predictable weekly job, burst is a good fit. We’d likely configure: baseline 8, max burst cap maybe +16 (so 24 total) depending on your tier, plus a cooldown policy if you hit saturation repeatedly.

[06:59] Sara Liu: We would prefer “cap by workload” though. Like indexing can use burst but chat shouldn’t.

[07:05] Mina Haddad: That’s a good requirement. Today our config is tenant-level, but we can approximate it by splitting routes—separate model endpoints or separate “routing groups”—and apply burst policy by route.

[07:18] Jon Peters: Can we actually enforce that? Because I can’t trust application teams to not accidentally send interactive traffic to the burst route.

[07:26] Mina Haddad: We can enforce via API keys / projects or via route-level policies in the control plane. It’s not “free” but it’s doable.

[07:36] Markus Klein: And in the Console you’d see per-route burst usage and denials.

[07:42] Sara Liu: That’s observability. What do you actually expose?

[07:46] Markus Klein: Several layers:
- Customer-facing: burst usage over time, current cap, current burst-in-use, and denial breakdown by reason.
- SRE/internal: pool saturation, queue depth, telemetry lag, neighbor impact metrics.

[08:04] Jon Peters: “Neighbor impact” makes me nervous. Are you going to show me other tenants?

[08:08] Markus Klein: No, it’s aggregated. Like “non-burst p95 delta in pool” or “tail amplification indicator.” Nothing identifying.

[08:16] Sara Liu: Is it Prometheus metrics? Or only dashboards.

[08:19] Markus Klein: Internally it’s Prometheus. Externally, you’ll see it in Console, and we can export a report.

[08:27] Mina Haddad: Also headers. For denied requests we can include a response header with the denial code and a recommended retry-after.

[08:35] Jon Peters: Please do. That helps support.

[08:38] Stephanie Nguyen: On the support side, we also have an internal debug endpoint so Support can explain “why did this request get denied.” With redaction.

[08:47] Amit Desai: That’s actually big for us. We’ve had other vendors just say “capacity.”

[08:53] Sara Liu: What about “mid-stream.” Like if a long generation starts under burst, can you revoke it?

[08:59] Mina Haddad: We don’t preempt in-flight requests for initial version. Admission is at start. Once admitted, it runs. We might clamp future admissions.

[09:09] Jon Peters: Okay good.

[09:11] Markus Klein: That’s part of determinism too.

[09:13] Sara Liu: How is fairness enforced? If a bigger customer bursts, do we get starved?

[09:18] Markus Klein: We use a token bucket style fairness with tiers. Each tenant earns burst tokens at a rate depending on tier and baseline size, and spends tokens when using burst. That prevents one tenant from monopolizing.

[09:33] Sara Liu: So it’s like weighted fair queueing.

[09:36] Markus Klein: Exactly, a hybrid. The goal is measurable: no starvation, bounded variance.

[09:42] Jon Peters: What’s the granularity? Like per second?

[09:45] Markus Klein: It’s evaluated on short intervals, e.g., 1–5 seconds, plus smoothing.

[09:52] Amit Desai: That seems pretty fast.

[09:54] Mina Haddad: We need fast because tail latency is fast.

[09:57] Sara Liu: Billing: how do you charge? Tokens? GPU seconds?

[10:02] Stephanie Nguyen: Still being finalized, but directionally: baseline is your reserved commit. Burst is metered separately—likely burst GPU-seconds and/or burst tokens processed. It’ll be a line item.

[10:15] Sara Liu: We’d rather not have two different metrics.

[10:18] Markus Klein: We hear that. The reason GPU-seconds shows up is it maps to actual cost. But we can present it as “burst token premium” for simplicity.

[10:29] Jon Peters: As long as we can reconcile it.

[10:31] Markus Klein: Reconciliation is a requirement. Also idempotency keys so retries don’t double count.

[10:39] Sara Liu: Do you have a concept of “burst budget” per month?

[10:43] Stephanie Nguyen: Likely yes as part of packaging—like included burst up to N, then overage. But we’ll bring Finance in.

[10:52] Amit Desai: Cool.

[10:55] Markus Klein: Let’s talk about routing and fallbacks. Mina, want to cover?

[10:59] Mina Haddad: Sure. In the data plane, every request gets a capacity decision: baseline vs burst. If burst is allowed, we can route to the burst pool. If not, we can do one of three things: (1) stay on baseline and accept slower throughput; (2) return 429 with reason; (3) for batch, queue. We also keep region fixed in v1—no cross-region bursting.

[11:21] Sara Liu: That’s okay. We want data residency anyway.

[11:24] Jon Peters: What about GPU type fallback? Like H100 to L40S.

[11:28] Mina Haddad: Not automatically for Dedicated burst. We want performance predictability. We can discuss as an explicit opt-in policy.

[11:37] Sara Liu: Good.

[11:39] Amit Desai: If we’re denied burst, we’d prefer it to just run slower, not error. For indexing. For online, better to error fast.

[11:48] Mina Haddad: That’s consistent with what we’re building. We can have route-specific behavior.

[11:53] Markus Klein: Observability again matters here because you’ll want to know “we slowed because burst denied.”

[12:00] Sara Liu: Do you expose “current burst available” like an API so we can plan?

[12:05] Markus Klein: We can expose your current cap and usage. We do not want to expose “pool free capacity” because that creates racing behavior across tenants.

[12:14] Jon Peters: Yeah, it turns into a thundering herd.

[12:16] Markus Klein: Exactly.

[12:18] Sara Liu: But at least tell us if we’re in cooldown.

[12:21] Mina Haddad: Yes. Denial reason code COOLDOWN_ACTIVE, and in Console you’d see timer.

[12:28] Amit Desai: Talk to me about audit logs. We have compliance folks.

[12:32] Markus Klein: Any burst config changes are audited: enable/disable, cap changes, tier changes, admin overrides. The audit event includes who did it (RBAC principal) and when, plus old/new values.

[12:47] Jon Peters: Can Support override without us knowing?

[12:50] Markus Klein: They can only if you grant that role, and it would be audited. Also we’re building a support-debug endpoint for “why admitted/denied” that’s internal only.

[13:03] Sara Liu: Okay.

[13:05] Stephanie Nguyen: We’re SOC 2 and have standard security docs. We can send those after.

[13:10] Sara Liu: Great.

[13:12] Markus Klein: I’m going to pause and ask: what are your “must-haves” for you to buy Dedicated with burst?

[13:18] Sara Liu: Must have: route-level burst policy or some way to isolate indexing from online. Must have: clear denial semantics and recommended retry behavior. Must have: reporting we can show internally.

[13:33] Jon Peters: For me: no “mystery latency.” If tail goes up, I want to see correlation to burst saturation and have confidence you clamp it.

[13:41] Amit Desai: And cost. Like it can’t be surprise spend.

[13:44] Stephanie Nguyen: Understood.

[13:46] Markus Klein: Great. On the first one, we can likely implement per-route burst settings by leveraging routing groups and policy evaluation. It’s a bit of config but it’s doable.

[13:59] Mina Haddad: To be clear, we’ll need you to separate API keys or endpoints so we can enforce it.

[14:05] Sara Liu: That’s okay.

[14:07] Markus Klein: On semantics, we’ll send a doc that spells out: what constitutes burst, how we decide, and what errors you’ll see.

[14:16] Jon Peters: Please include the reason codes.

[14:18] Markus Klein: Yep.

[14:20] Stephanie Nguyen: On cost, we’ll schedule pricing follow-up. We can propose a tier that matches 2–3x for 2 hours weekly.

[14:31] Amit Desai: Cool.

[14:33] Sara Liu: What about SLAs? Is burst covered?

[14:36] Stephanie Nguyen: Baseline Dedicated SLA is one thing. Burst is best-effort with guardrails. We’ll have contract language that clarifies it’s not guaranteed capacity.

[14:49] Jon Peters: That’s fine, as long as baseline is protected.

[14:52] Markus Klein: Exactly. Baseline is what we guarantee.

[14:56] Sara Liu: Timeline? Like when can we try this.

[14:59] Stephanie Nguyen: We’re targeting internal beta in May, GA-ish in June. We can potentially get you into a limited beta depending on region and hardware availability.

[15:12] Amit Desai: We’re aiming for Q2 anyway.

[15:15] Markus Klein: Great. We’ll want your workload profile to size it and to set initial caps.

[15:21] Sara Liu: We can provide tokens per request and concurrency.

[15:24] Jon Peters: We also have our own load test harness.

[15:27] Markus Klein: Perfect.

[15:29] Mina Haddad: One more subtle point: If you’re doing batch, you might run into a scenario where you are admitted but slower than expected because fairness is enforcing smoothing. That’s not a “deny” but you’ll see throughput shaping.

[15:45] Sara Liu: Is that visible?

[15:47] Mina Haddad: It should be. “Admitted under throttle” kind of state. We’re still deciding how to expose that, but we don’t want it hidden.

[15:57] Jon Peters: You said earlier no cross-region. But what about multi-AZ within region.

[16:02] Markus Klein: Yes, within region we do multi-AZ and we balance. Burst pool is regional.

[16:08] Sara Liu: Good.

[16:10] Markus Klein: Anything else you’re worried about?

[16:13] Jon Peters: Telemetry lag. You mentioned earlier it can cause unfair denials.

[16:17] Markus Klein: Yeah. We’re specifically adding protections: smoothing windows, minimum hold times for decisions, and we’ll treat “telemetry stale” as a separate reason so it’s explainable.

[16:30] Jon Peters: Okay. Because I’ve seen systems where lag equals chaos.

[16:33] Mina Haddad: Same. That’s why we’re designing it to degrade safely.

[16:37] Sara Liu: What’s the API surface? Do we set burst caps via a control plane config?

[16:42] Markus Klein: Yes. Tenant config has: burst_enabled, max_burst_ratio, absolute_burst_cap, cooldown settings, and priority tier.

[16:55] Sara Liu: Priority tier—like gold/silver.

[16:58] Markus Klein: Exactly. But with constraints to prevent starvation.

[17:03] Amit Desai: Sounds like a lot of knobs.

[17:05] Markus Klein: We’ll ship sane defaults. Most customers will have like two or three parameters.

[17:12] Stephanie Nguyen: And CS will help with setup.

[17:15] Sara Liu: Great.

[17:17] Markus Klein: Let’s do a quick recap of requirements I heard: route isolation, clear denial reason codes + retry-after, console reporting, and strict non-burst SLO protection.

[17:30] Amit Desai: Yes.

[17:31] Jon Peters: Add: audit logs and “support can explain it.”

[17:35] Markus Klein: Yep.

[17:37] Stephanie Nguyen: Alright. I’ll tee up next steps. Markus will send the semantics doc and reason codes. Mina will share dashboard examples. And we’ll schedule pricing and SRE follow-ups.

[17:49] Sara Liu: Works.

[17:51] (crosstalk)

[17:53] Jon Peters: One more thing—what status code for deny.

[17:56] Mina Haddad: Likely 429 for “cap reached” and “pool saturated,” with a structured body and headers. For some internal paths it might be 503, but we’ll standardize.

[18:09] Jon Peters: Okay.

[18:10] Stephanie Nguyen: Great. We’ve got like 10 minutes left. Anything else?

[18:14] Sara Liu: Can procurement join for the pricing call.

[18:17] Stephanie Nguyen: Yes. Speaking of—if Nina is on, hi Nina.

[18:21] Nina Patel: Hi, sorry, I joined late. Just listening. I’ll want to understand if burst is a committed add-on or true usage-based.

[18:29] Stephanie Nguyen: Totally. We’ll cover both options.

[18:32] Markus Klein: And we’ll provide a reconciliation story so billing makes sense.

[18:36] Nina Patel: Perfect.

[18:39] Stephanie Nguyen: Okay. We’ll follow up by email with times and materials. Thanks everyone.

[18:46] Amit Desai: Thanks.

[18:47] Sara Liu: Thanks.

[18:48] Jon Peters: Appreciate it.

[18:50] Meeting ended (Fireflies).
